title: 16 Week Marathon Training Plan (Miles & Km)
excerpt: Every week of a 16-week marathon schedule in miles and km, with a goal-pace key. For runners at 25-30 mi (40-48 km) a week; peaks at 48 mi (77 km).
body:
16 Week Marathon Training Plan (Miles & Km)

This 16 week marathon training plan is for runners who already run about 25–30 miles (40–48 km) a week, including a long run of at least 10 miles (16 km), and want a structured four-month build to race day. It gives you every week of the schedule in miles and kilometres, a pace key based on your goal marathon pace, and clear rules for adjusting it.

The plan uses five runs a week and peaks at 48 miles (77 km), with a 21-mile (34 km) long run three weeks before the race. Not sure 16 weeks is the right length for you? Compare all our marathon plans here.

Who this plan is for

Start this plan if all of these are true:

  • You have run 4–5 days a week, totalling 25–30 miles (40–48 km), for at least the last month.
  • Your current long run is 10–11 miles (16–18 km) and it feels comfortable.
  • You have finished a half marathon, or could run one today, without pain.
  • Your race is 16 weeks away. One spare week in hand is useful in case of illness.

If your weekly mileage is lower, start with the 20 week plan or the 6 month plan. If this is your first marathon and you only run three or four times a week, the 18-week beginner plan is a better fit. If you have a specific time goal of under four hours, the sub 4 hour plan uses the same 16 weeks with exact paces.

The full 16-week schedule (miles & km)

Each row is one week, from Monday to Sunday. Monday and Friday are rest days. Tuesday is the main workout. Thursday becomes a marathon-pace run from week 5. Sunday is the long run. You can move days to fit your week, as long as there is a rest or easy day between hard sessions.

Pace key

  • Easy: conversational, about 60–90 s/mi (35–55 s/km) slower than goal marathon pace.
  • Long run: easy pace, 45–90 s/mi (30–55 s/km) slower than goal marathon pace, except segments marked @ MP.
  • MP: your goal marathon pace.
  • T (threshold): comfortably hard, the pace you could race for about an hour. Roughly 25–40 s/mi (15–25 s/km) faster than MP. Jog 2 min between reps.
  • I (intervals): 5K–10K effort, roughly 50–80 s/mi (30–50 s/km) faster than MP. Jog 90 s–2 min between reps.
  • Hills: 60 s uphill at 5K effort; jog back down.
  • Strides: 20 s quick and relaxed at the end of an easy run. Walk back to recover.
  • Workout distances include a 1–2 mi (2–3 km) warm-up and cool-down.

How the 16 weeks are built

Weeks 1–4: base

Mileage starts close to what you already run (29 miles / 47 km) and rises by no more than about 10% a week. One short threshold session and one interval session reintroduce faster running. Week 4 is a cutback week, dropping to 27 miles (43 km), so your body can absorb the first block.

Weeks 5–8: build

Marathon-pace (MP) running starts on Thursdays: 4–5 miles (6–8 km) at goal pace inside a longer run. Tuesday alternates between threshold and interval sessions, and the long run reaches 16 miles (26 km). Week 8 is another cutback.

Weeks 9–13: marathon-specific

This is the hardest block. MP segments grow to 7 miles (11 km), and the week-10 long run ends with 3 miles at goal pace. Weekly volume peaks at 48 miles (77 km) in weeks 11 and 13, with a cutback in week 12 between them. The longest run, 21 miles (34 km) at easy pace, comes in week 13, three weeks before race day. That leaves enough time to recover from it before the race.

Weeks 14–16: taper

Volume falls from 48 to 39, then 31, then 15 miles (77, 63, 50 and 24 km), and race week is the lightest. Short, sharp sessions stay in the plan so your legs keep their speed while fatigue clears. Don't add extra runs here: you gain nothing in the last two weeks except freshness.

How to adjust the plan

  • Running in kilometres: follow the km figures. They are rounded, so a day off by 1 km makes no difference.
  • Setting your goal pace: take a recent half-marathon time, multiply it by about 2.1, and add 5–10 minutes if this is your first marathon. For example, 1:50 × 2.1 is about 3:51, so a first marathon goal would be about 3:56–4:01. Use that pace for every MP session.
  • You have 17–20 weeks: repeat weeks 1–3 before starting week 4, or follow the 20 week plan instead.
  • Only four days a week: drop the Wednesday easy run. The peak week becomes about 42 miles (68 km), which is still enough to race well.
  • Missed training: after up to a week off for illness, pick up where the calendar says, but run the first workout easy. After two or more weeks off, repeat the last full week you completed before moving on. Never squeeze missed miles into the following week.
  • Struggling: if easy runs feel hard for several days, or your resting heart rate stays high, turn Thursday into an easy run and repeat the week.
  • Hilly course: run Tuesday sessions and some long runs on rolling routes from week 9 onward.
  • Pain or injury: pain that changes how you run, or doesn't ease within a few days, means stop and see a doctor or physio. Don't run through it.

Fueling, strength and race week

From week 9, take carbohydrate on every long run over 90 minutes, using the gels or drinks you plan to race with. Do two short strength sessions a week through week 12, on rest or easy days, then drop to one during the taper. In race week, eat more carbohydrate for the final two days. For targets and examples, see our guide to what a marathon plan should include.

Related plans

  • Sub 4 hour marathon training plan: also 16 weeks, with exact paces for a 3:59 finish.
  • 20 week marathon training plan: a lower starting base and a longer runway.
  • Intermediate marathon training plan: 18 weeks, peaking at 55 miles, for runners who have already done a marathon.

FAQ

Is 16 weeks enough to train for a marathon?

Yes, if you start with a base of about 25–30 miles (40–48 km) a week and can already run 10 miles. Sixteen weeks leaves time for three build blocks and a three-week taper. If you are starting from under 15 miles a week, 16 weeks is tight. A 20 week or 6 month plan lowers your injury risk.

Can a beginner use a 16 week marathon plan?

A first-time marathoner can, as long as they already have the base above. Many first-timers don't, and for them the 18-week beginner plan starts lower and uses four runs a week.

How many miles a week is a 16 week marathon training plan?

This plan runs from 29 miles (47 km) in week 1 to a peak of 48 miles (77 km) in weeks 11 and 13, with cutback weeks of 27–36 miles (43–58 km) in between.

What is the longest run in a 16 week plan?

The longest run is 21 miles (34 km), in week 13. You don't need to run 26.2 miles in training. A run of about 20 miles, plus weeks of consistent volume and a proper taper, prepares you for the full distance.
keyTakeaway: Sixteen weeks is enough if you already run 25-30 miles a week with a 10-mile long run: three build blocks, a 21-mile peak long run and a three-week taper.
